transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The balance of power in Congress has shifted back to Democrats.
Some midterm results are still coming in, including in Alaska and Mississippi.
But the Democrats have secured a solid majority flipping at least 28 House seats despite GOP
redistricting efforts.
They've also flipped at least seven Senate seats in Kansas, Iowa, Maine, North Carolina,
South Carolina, Texas, and Ohio.
President Trump drove the push for preemptive redistricting in a bid to fend off the usual
midterm reckoning, but NPR's Ashley Lopez reports those efforts failed in several cases.
Democrats won congressional districts that were redrawn by the GOP for the explicit purpose
of giving their party an edge in this year's election.
Republicans were bracing for some losses this cycle, so President Trump urged his party
to take the extraordinary step of engaging in mid-decade redistricting efforts.
But in Florida, North Carolina, Alabama, and Texas, Democrats were able to win many of
those redrawn districts.
Republicans redrew their maps with the expectation that the coalition of voters who Trump won
over in 2024 would support him this cycle.
But many of those voters shifted their support to Democrats this year.
Ashley Lopez, NPR News.
NPR's Hansi Lo Wang says tens of millions of voters got to the polls yesterday on top
of the nearly 62 million who voted early.
Around the country, early in-person and mail-in voters cast 35 percent more ballots compared
to the last midterm general elections in 2022, as according to the latest data compiled by
the University of Florida's election lab.
It will take days for some states to finish reviewing provisional ballots and accepting
mail-in ballots postmarked by election day.
But there are early signs that the U.S. may have seen one of the highest voter turnout
rates for a midterm general election since direct general elections of U.S. senators by
popular vote began in 1914.
The current record holder is the 2018 election, the midterms of the first Trump administration.
Hansi Lo Wang, NPR News.
Well, Florida remains a slight bright spot for Republicans, where they retain control
of the governor and Senate seats and seem to have held on to a number of competitive
seats.
But they have not yet picked up a seat they redrew in mid-decade redistricting and do
not appear poised to do so.
Well, among the Democrats who won House and Senate seats, a surprising number of clergy
and clergy-in-training, more from NPR's Jason DeRose.
In recent decades, Republicans have often seemed more comfortable talking about religion,
but this midterm election year was different.
Heading to the U.S. Senate, Adam Hamilton is a pastor of a large United Methodist congregation
in Kansas and Texas state representative James Tallarico, who's also a Presbyterian seminarian.
Heading to the U.S. House, there's Frederick Haines, pastor of a 13,000-member Baptist
church in the Dallas area.
Sarah Trone-Garytt is a state senator from the Des Moines area in Iowa and a Lutheran
pastor.
Also in Iowa, Congresswoman-elect Lindsay James is a Presbyterian chaplain from Dubuque
and a state House representative.
That's Jason DeRose reporting.
It's NPR News.
U.S. allies overseas have been closely watching the midterm results.
NPR's Emily Fang reports on the election's impact on U.S. foreign policy.
News in the Middle East, including Israel, are now waiting to see if President Trump
will escalate the war in Iran, or if a bluer Congress will successfully pressure the White
House to end the conflict.
The big terms were also news in Japan and the Philippines.
Two U.S. allies who have seen U.S. defense resources diverted to the Middle East in the
last year.
And Asia's Taiwan is hoping a series of long-delayed American arms sales will finally be delivered
now that Democrats will control Congress.
The countries like South Korea, with big companies whose fortunes are tied to the U.S. A.I. boom,
are anxious.
Democratic-backed moratoriums and data center construction could hurt their bottom lines.
Emily Fang, NPR News, the White House.
CVS Health is dividing into two companies, splitting apart its pharmacies and its insurance
business.
Details from NPR's Alina Seljuk.
CVS put Adna in caremark under its one roof in 2018, creating a conglomerate reaching
into many corners of healthcare.
And this marked an era of ballooning healthcare giants, including rivals United Health and
Cigna.
Lately, these companies have faced growing scrutiny from state and federal regulators
and lawmakers over the role in rising health costs.
And the pharmacy business has become tricky with changing drug prices and American spending
habits.
Now, CVS says it's splitting back up.
One company will be the retail pharmacy business.
The other will be Adna and Caremark doing insurance and pharmacy benefit management.
The announcement says this will help each of the two better focus on their unique goals.
Alina Seljuk, NPR News.
This is NPR News.

topics.text: Democrats win House majority and flip at least seven Senate seats in midterm elections
Republican mid-decade redistricting efforts fail in Florida, North Carolina, Alabama, and Texas
Midterm voter turnout appears among highest for a midterm since 1914, per early data
Florida Republicans keep governor and Senate seats but fail to gain redrawn districts
Several Democratic midterm winners are pastors, clergy, or seminarians, including Adam Hamilton and Frederick Haines
US allies Japan, Philippines, Taiwan, and South Korea watch midterms for impact on defense and tech
CVS Health splits into two companies, separating retail pharmacy from Aetna and Caremark insurance
